n: Amos sings a funeral song over Israel, even while the nation is still alive and prosperous. Announcing a funeral for the living was a shocking way to warn them.

f.g: A funeral dirge, sung in a distinctive limping rhythm in Hebrew.

n: Israel is pictured as a young woman who has fallen and has no one to lift her up.

f.g: A poetic personification of the nation.

n: War will cut Israel’s armies down to a tenth. A town that sent a thousand soldiers will see only a hundred return.
The heart of Amos’s message: seek the Lord and live. Life comes from a relationship with God, not from rituals.

f.w: Seek ye me, and ye shall live

n: Don’t look for God at the popular shrines of Bethel, Gilgal, and Beersheba. There are wordplays: Gilgal will go into exile (galoh yigleh) and Bethel will become nothing.

f.g: A town far south in Judah; northerners made pilgrimages there.
Bethel (“house of God”) will become Beth-aven (“house of nothing”), as Hosea 4:15 puns.

n: Seek the Lord and live — or His judgment will spread through Israel like fire that Bethel’s gods can’t put out.

f.g: The northern kingdom, led by Joseph’s descendants Ephraim and Manasseh.

n: Those who make justice bitter and cast righteousness to the ground are addressed. Justice that should heal has become poison.

f.g: A very bitter plant; a symbol of bitterness and sorrow.
Justice, fair rulings.

n: Seek the Creator who placed the star clusters, turns deep darkness into dawn, and pours the sea’s waters on the land. The same God who controls nature will judge.

f.g: The Pleiades cluster and the constellation Orion.
Deepest darkness.

f.w: calleth for the waters of the sea

n: God can suddenly empower the weak and plundered against the strong, so that even fortresses fall.

f.g: Destruction, ruin (or those who have been plundered).

n: The powerful hate anyone who stands up for justice at the city gate, where court cases were heard.

f.g: The city gate was the public courthouse and marketplace.

n: Because they tax the poor heavily, their fine stone houses and vineyards will not benefit them. They will lose what they gained unfairly.

f.g: Heavy grain levies or rents.

f.w: ye shall not dwell in them

n: God sees their many sins: persecuting the innocent, taking bribes, and denying the poor their rights in court.
In such a corrupt time, wise people keep quiet — or perhaps they will be stunned into silence when disaster comes.

f.g: The wise or shrewd.

n: Seek what is good, not evil, and live. Then the Lord really will be with you, as you already claim He is.

f.g: Israel boasted that God was on their side; Amos says that is true only if they seek good.

n: Hate evil, love good, and make the courts fair. Perhaps the Lord will be gracious to what remains of Israel. Amos offers hope, but no guarantee.

f.w: Hate the evil, and love the good

n: Because they won’t repent, mourning will fill the streets. Even farmers will be called to wail alongside professional mourners.

f.g: Professional mourners hired for funerals.

n: Even the vineyards — normally places of joyful harvest songs — will hear wailing, because the Lord will pass through in judgment, as He once passed through Egypt.
Israel looked forward to “the day of the Lord” as a day of victory. Amos warns: for the wicked, it will be darkness, not light.
A vivid picture: escaping a lion only to meet a bear, then reaching home and leaning on the wall — and a snake bites you. There is no escape.

f.g: An image of danger striking where one feels safest.

n: Amos repeats for emphasis: the day of the Lord will be pitch dark, without a glimmer of light, for those unprepared.
Strong words: God hates their religious festivals. Worship without justice and mercy disgusts Him.

f.g: God will not accept the aroma of their sacrifices.

f.w: I hate, I despise your feast days

n: Burnt offerings, grain offerings, and fattened peace offerings — God will accept none of them, since they come from unrepentant hearts.

f.g: Grain offerings.

n: Stop the noisy hymns and harp music! Beautiful worship music means nothing to God when hearts are unjust.

f.g: Harps or lyres; stringed instruments.

n: Amos’s most famous line: let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream. God wants justice that never dries up. Martin Luther King Jr. quoted it in the civil rights movement.

f.w: let judgment run down as waters

f.g: An ever-flowing stream — unlike wadis that dry up in summer.

n: God asks: during the forty years in the wilderness, did you really offer Me sacrifices from the heart? The question suggests their worship was compromised even then.
They carried idols of foreign star gods along with them. Stephen quoted this verse in his defense before the Sanhedrin.

f.g: Probably Sakkuth, an Assyrian god; the Greek translation reads “Moloch.”
Probably Kaiwan, an Assyrian name for the planet Saturn, worshiped as a god.

n: Therefore Israel will go into exile beyond Damascus — that is, to Assyria. This happened in 722 BC.
